label: Person
name: Abundius of Como
summary:
Abundius of Como (died c. 469) was Bishop of Como in northern Italy and an important figure in the theological controversies of the fifth century, particularly the Nestorian controversy and its aftermath. Born near Thessalonica of Greek parents, he had Greek as his first language, which made him valuable as an intermediary between the Latin West and the Greek East at a moment of intense theological exchange.

Abundius served as a papal legate sent by Pope Leo I ('the Great') to the Eastern Court at Constantinople, where he participated in the negotiations surrounding the Council of Chalcedon (451). He carried Leo's famous 'Tome' — the doctrinal letter defining Christ's two natures — to the East and played an active diplomatic role in securing Chalcedon's acceptance. His Greek linguistic competence and diplomatic skill made him an invaluable intermediary for Leo's theological programme.

His papally delegated mission to the East placed him at the centre of the most important Christological definition in Church history. The Council of Chalcedon's Definition of the Two Natures of Christ in one Person became the foundational statement of orthodox Christology for both East and West, and Abundius's participation in its reception was significant. He is venerated as a saint with a feast day on 2 April.
